name: Puma http11_parser (Mongrel/Ragel-based HTTP/1.x parser)
workload: Repeatedly parsing a single realistic HTTP/1.1 GET request (headers only, no body) 3,000,000 and 5,000,000 times, comparing nginx-derived joyent/http-parser (http_parser.c) against Puma's Ragel-generated http11 parser (originally Zed Shaw's Mongrel parser).
claimed_speedup: ~1.26x faster: 3.215s vs 4.065s (http-parser) for 3M iterations; 5.359s vs 6.778s for 5M iterations (wall-clock `time`)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2407 @ 2.20GHz (per /proc/cpuinfo pasted in README)
stars_or_usage: 7.9k stars (puma); benchmark repo itself has 2 stars
tradeoffs: Ragel-generated state machine (needs Ragel toolchain to regenerate from .rl source); handles only the request-line/header tokenizing role used by Puma/Mongrel/Unicorn/Thin, not full HTTP semantics (chunked/body handling done by caller); embedded as ext/puma_http11 inside the puma gem rather than shipped as a standalone library.
caveats: Benchmark repo (jiakai1000/httpparsers) is tiny (2 stars) and unmaintained since May 2025; states CPU model but not compiler or optimization flags, and uses coarse wall-clock `time` over a single repeated request rather than a varied corpus, so results are indicative, not rigorous.
found_via: gh search repos "http parser" benchmark --sort stars --limit 30 -> jiakai1000/httpparsers (shootout repo comparing http_parser.c vs http11_parser.c)

name: Ada (WHATWG URL parser)
workload: Validating and normalizing thousands of real-world URLs harvested from the top 100 popular websites (ada-url/url-various-datasets top100 corpus), measuring nanoseconds per URL.
claimed_speedup: ~7.8x faster than CURL's URL parser (188 ns/URL vs 1471 ns/URL) and ~3.5x faster than servo/rust-url (188 ns/URL vs 664 ns/URL); separately reported up to 400% URL-parsing speedup in Node.js after Ada replaced its prior parser (State of Node.js Performance 2023)
stars_or_usage: 1.85k stars; used in Node.js, ClickHouse, Redpanda, Kong, Telegram, Adguard, Datadog, Cloudflare Workers, Internet Archive
tradeoffs: URL parsing/validation only (not HTTP header/request-line parsing); WHATWG-URL-standard semantics differ subtly from RFC 3986 parsers, which can matter for strict compliance; requires C++20 compiler.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (project's own README/benchmarks dir) though backed by a peer-reviewed paper (Nizipli & Lemire, 'Parsing Millions of URLs per Second', Software: Practice and Experience 54(5), 2024, https://doi.org/10.1002/spe.3296); hardware is stated only as 'Apple MacBook 2022' without exact CPU/SoC model, and full compiler flags are not given, so capped below tier A.
found_via: gh api repos/ada-url/ada/readme performance section, following up from KNOWN_LIST entry ada-url/idna (sibling project) which pointed to the main ada-url/ada repo not itself on KNOWN_LIST

name: iohttpparser (stateful-strict/lenient profiles)
workload: req/s, MiB/s and ns/req for parsing 20 request/response fixture scenarios (small requests, header-heavy requests/responses, upgrade responses, CONNECT requests, header-name/value stress cases) as a repeated keep-alive byte stream, ~8GiB decoded fixture data per case, median of 5 runs, comparing iohttpparser's four profiles against picohttpparser and llhttp v-current.
claimed_speedup: iohttpparser profiles beat llhttp on most full-message scenarios, e.g. req-headers 9.12M vs 7.87M req/s (1.16x), resp-headers 12.08M vs 9.55M req/s (1.26x), hdr-value-ascii-clean 7.72M vs 5.16M req/s (1.50x), hdr-count-32-minimal 2.89M vs 1.93M req/s (1.50x); loses to llhttp on several request-line-only micro-scenarios (e.g. req-line-only, req-line-connect); picohttpparser remains the fastest of the three in every scenario.
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.0, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with CMAKE_INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION=ON, -fuse-ld=lld -flto=thin (clang-release CMake preset)
hardware: AMD EPYC Processor, 8 vCPU, KVM-virtualized host (per host.txt in the run artifact)
tradeoffs: Pull-based API with explicit parser state and a separate semantics/body-decoder stage, unlike llhttp's callback-driven model; adds framing-ambiguity rejection (TE+CL, conflicting Content-Length) that llhttp only partially covers; consistently slower than picohttpparser across all measured scenarios.
caveats: Zero-star, single-contributor project published March 2026 with no independent adoption or third-party reproduction; benchmark hardware is a KVM-virtualized AMD EPYC instance (likely a shared CI/cloud runner), which adds noise versus bare-metal; wins over llhttp are inconsistent across scenarios (llhttp wins several request-line-only micro-benchmarks), so this is not a uniform speedup.
found_via: gh search repos "http/1.1 parser" --sort stars --limit 30 -> ioplane/iohttpparser, then docs/en/09-test-results.md and tests/artifacts/pmi-psi/runs/.../summary.md

name: httparse (Rust push parser for HTTP/1.x)
workload: Not specified by the project; the claim is a general statement about parsing HTTP/1.x requests/responses, not tied to a stated corpus or iteration count.
claimed_speedup: "The speed is faster than picohttpparser, when SIMD is not available." (no numeric figure given; claim present in published crate version 1.2.3's lib.rs doc comment, no longer present in the current README/lib.rs which instead says SIMD is enabled automatically)
stars_or_usage: 714 GitHub stars; the de facto HTTP/1.x parser for Rust, used by hyper, actix-web, and most of the Rust HTTP ecosystem
tradeoffs: no_std-friendly, allocation-free, push-style API (caller supplies header-slot buffer); safety-critical `unsafe` is scoped to a single submodule; the historical picohttpparser claim is explicitly qualified to only the no-SIMD case, which is increasingly rare since SIMD paths are now auto-detected at runtime.
caveats: No numbers are given for the claim anywhere in the project's history I could find (checked current README, current lib.rs, benches/parse.rs, and CHANGELOG; only found the qualitative sentence in the old published 1.2.3 source, vendored in third-party dependency mirrors). Included at tier D only because the project is extremely widely used (hyper's default parser).
found_via: gh search code "faster than picohttpparser" -> vendored copies of httparse 1.2.3 src/lib.rs (e.g. mfarrugi/cargo-raze-example-stdx); verified against current seanmonstar/httparse source

name: fasthttp (Go HTTP server/client package)
workload: Go `testing` benchmark (`go test -bench`) serving/requesting a simple GET across varying requests-per-connection and client counts (1/2/10/10K reqs per conn, up to 10K clients), at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 4, comparing fasthttp's own hand-written zero-allocation HTTP parser/server against net/http's http.Server built on net/http's parser.
claimed_speedup: Up to 10x faster overall (README headline); server benchmark at GOMAXPROCS=4, 10K-reqs-per-connection: net/http 2179 ns/op (2386 B/op, 21 allocs/op) vs fasthttp 451.4 ns/op (0 B/op, 0 allocs/op) -- ~4.8x lower latency and zero allocations vs 21 allocs/op; at GOMAXPROCS=1 the same case is 7151 ns/op (net/http) vs 1422 ns/op (fasthttp), ~5x; client comparison claimed up to 4x faster.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.20GHz (exact model number not given; from `go test` output header)
stars_or_usage: 23.5k stars; also referenced in TechEmpower Benchmark round 23 plaintext results
tradeoffs: Deliberately breaks net/http API compatibility (custom RequestCtx-based API, no `net/http` Handler interface) to avoid allocations; reused/pooled request and response objects require careful lifetime handling (documented 'gotchas' around retaining pointers past handler return); benchmarks measure full request/response handling, not an isolated parser microbenchmark.
caveats: First-party benchmark (project's own go test bench code) with partial methodology: CPU model given only generically ('Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.20GHz', no exact SKU), no Go version or GOMAXPROCS-independent compiler flags stated beyond the command line shown; benchmark measures the whole request/response server path (allocations, routing) rather than isolating HTTP parsing.
found_via: gh search repos fasthttp --sort stars -> valyala/fasthttp README 'HTTP server performance comparison with net/http' section

name: sorug (WHATWG URL parser, Rust)
workload: Criterion benchmarks (release profile, lto=true, codegen-units=1) over four URL workloads: a simple ASCII URL, a URL with complex query/fragment, an IDNA/Punycode hostname, and a file-URL edge case; nanoseconds per parse.
claimed_speedup: vs servo/url (the incumbent Rust URL crate): ~3.4x on simple ASCII URLs (28.3ns vs 97ns), ~3.9x on complex query/fragment (56.0ns vs 216ns), ~1.27x on IDNA/Punycode (196ns vs 248ns), ~4.1x on file-URL edge cases (31.1ns vs 129ns). Also reported faster than ada-url on all four of the same workloads (e.g. 28.3ns vs 31.9ns fast path; 56.0ns vs 140ns complex query; 196ns vs 277ns IDNA; 31.1ns vs 95.0ns file edge case).
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile, lto=true, codegen-units=1 (Criterion harness)
tradeoffs: `forbid(unsafe_code)` (no unsafe in library code) unlike many fast parsers; no_std + alloc friendly; ships its own vendored Unicode/Punycode tables instead of depending on ICU/idna crate, which is a maintenance burden for Unicode updates; extremely new/unproven (single author, 1 star, published within days of this search).
caveats: README explicitly states 'Numbers are indicative. Absolute values vary by CPU; relative ordering is what we track' -- no CPU model or OS version is given at all, only 'Linux', so this falls short of tier B/A on hardware disclosure alone; entirely first-party, unreplicated benchmark from a brand-new (days-old) single-star repository.
found_via: gh search repos "url parser" simd -> hocestnonsatis/sorug README Benchmarks section
